title: Mercantilists & Physiocrats
description: Gold, balance of trade, Quesnay's tableau — economics before Smith

concepts.title: Mercantilism
concepts.contentHtml:
For about 250 years (1500-1750), the dominant European economic doctrine was mercantilism. The core view: a nation's wealth equals its stock of gold and silver. To get richer, accumulate precious metals through favorable balance of trade.

Implications: export more than you import. Restrict imports through tariffs and prohibitions. Subsidize exports. Develop colonies as captive markets and raw-material sources. Build naval power to protect trade.

Mercantilism wasn't a unified theory — it was a collection of policies and pamphlets reflecting the interests of merchants and emerging nation-states. But it shaped European economic policy through the age of exploration and early industrialization.

concepts.title: Why Mercantilism Was Wrong
concepts.contentHtml:
Mercantilism's central error: confusing money with wealth.

If a nation's gold stock doubles overnight, prices double too — real living standards don't change. David Hume's specie-flow mechanism (1752) showed: as gold flows in, domestic prices rise, exports become uncompetitive, gold flows out, equilibrium restored. Trade surpluses can't accumulate gold indefinitely.

The deeper error: viewing trade as zero-sum. If I gain by exporting, you must lose by importing. This rationalized hostile trade policy and frequent wars over commercial advantage.

Real wealth, as later economists would clarify, comes from production — useful goods and services — not metal in vaults. Trade is positive-sum: both sides gain when exchange is voluntary.

Mercantilist intuitions persist in modern policy debates: trade deficits as 'losing,' currency manipulation as 'beggar-thy-neighbor.' The classical refutation hasn't fully won the political argument.

concepts.title: The Physiocrats
concepts.contentHtml:
French Physiocrats in the 1750s-1770s developed an alternative theory: agriculture, not gold, is the source of wealth.

Their core claim: only land produces a 'net product' — output exceeding the labor and inputs used. Manufacturing and commerce just transform existing wealth; agriculture creates new wealth.

The intellectual leader François Quesnay was physician to Louis XV — bringing a circulation-of-blood metaphor to the economy. His Tableau Économique (1758) showed how output flows between landowners, farmers, and artisans — one of the first formal economic models.

Policy implications: tax only land (since it's the source of net product). Free trade in agricultural products. Liberal commerce.

Physiocrats were wrong about agriculture's special status — but right about flows, market liberalism, and tax efficiency. Their work directly influenced Adam Smith.

concepts.title: Laissez Faire
concepts.contentHtml:
The Physiocrats popularized the phrase laissez faire, laissez passer ('let do, let pass'), usually credited to their ally Gournay; 'laissez faire' itself traces to the merchant Legendre around 1680. Government should let markets operate freely.

The argument was less ideological than empirical. Quesnay observed that price controls, trade restrictions, and guild monopolies produced visible inefficiency and distress. Liberal commerce produced visible prosperity.

This was a radical claim in 18th-century Europe, where extensive regulation was the norm — guilds controlled who could practice trades, internal tolls choked commerce, royal monopolies privileged the well-connected.

The laissez-faire argument set up later debates: when does government intervention help, when does it hurt? Smith built on this; Marx criticized it; Keynes qualified it. The basic question — when should markets work alone? — has been with economics ever since.

concepts.title: Why History of Economics Matters
concepts.contentHtml:
Why study old, mostly-superseded ideas?

Because economics is partly a science of arguments as much as facts. The same disagreements recur — under different terminology, with different evidence, in different contexts. Understanding the lineage clarifies current debates.

Mercantilist intuitions appear in modern protectionism. Physiocratic enthusiasm for land taxes appears in the Henry George movement. Laissez-faire arguments resurface in every regulatory debate.

Knowing the history doesn't decide current questions, but it shows which arguments have been tried, what failed, what worked, and under what conditions. The economic ideas of 1776 (Smith), 1817 (Ricardo), 1867 (Marx), 1936 (Keynes), and 1970s (Friedman, Lucas) all still affect 2025 policy debates — sometimes openly, often unconsciously.

title: Classical: Smith & Ricardo
description: Invisible hand, division of labor, comparative advantage, the labor theory of value

concepts.title: Adam Smith and The Wealth of Nations
concepts.contentHtml:
Adam Smith's An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (1776) is the foundational text of modern economics.

Smith broke decisively with mercantilism. Wealth, he argued, comes from production — labor making useful things — not from gold. National wealth equals output, which depends on labor productivity, which depends on the division of labor and capital accumulation.

The book ranges over markets, prices, wages, profits, taxation, public goods, education, colonial policy. It's part economics, part political economy, part philosophy of human nature. The integrated treatment defined economics as a discipline.

Smith was not a doctrinaire libertarian. He distrusted businessmen ('seldom meet together... but the conversation ends in a conspiracy against the public') and supported significant government roles in defense, justice, infrastructure, and education.

concepts.title: The Invisible Hand
concepts.contentHtml:
Smith's most-quoted metaphor: the invisible hand. Each individual pursuing private gain is led 'as if by an invisible hand' to advance public interest, which formed no part of their intention.

The mechanism: in competitive markets, prices coordinate production with consumption. Self-interest produces what consumers want, at competitive prices, without central direction.

Smith used the phrase three times in his work — far less prominent in his actual writings than in popular memory. He was making a specific point about how markets aggregate disparate self-interest into beneficial outcomes — not claiming markets always work.

The First Welfare Theorem of 20th-century mathematical economics is the rigorous version: under specific assumptions (perfect competition, complete markets, no externalities, perfect information), competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient.

Smith's intuition runs through modern economics. The invisible hand is one of the most powerful and most misused concepts in social science.

concepts.title: Division of Labor
concepts.contentHtml:
Smith opens Wealth of Nations with a pin factory. A single craftsman might produce 20 pins in a day. With ten workers, each specialized — one drawing wire, one straightening, one cutting, one pointing, one grinding — they produce 48,000 pins per day. Specialization multiplies productivity.

Three reasons: workers develop skill at one task, save time switching between tasks, and develop tools to improve specific operations.

The implication: productivity grows with the extent of the market. Larger markets allow finer division of labor, which raises productivity, which raises wealth.

This single insight does an enormous amount of work. It explains why cities are productive (concentration enables specialization), why trade benefits (extends the market), why poor countries can be productive (labor-intensive specialization), why technology matters (tools embodying division of labor).

Modern economics' attention to scale economies, network effects, and productivity decomposition all has roots in this insight.

concepts.title: David Ricardo's Comparative Advantage
concepts.contentHtml:
David Ricardo's On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (1817) systematized and extended Smith.

His most-celebrated contribution: comparative advantage. Even when one country is more productive at everything, both gain from trade as long as their productivity ratios differ.

Ricardo's classic example: England trades cloth for Portuguese wine. Even if Portugal can produce both more efficiently, both countries are better off when each specializes in their comparative advantage and trades.

The insight is non-obvious. Most people instinctively reason in terms of absolute advantage — 'we should make what we're best at.' Comparative advantage shows that's wrong: countries should make what they're relatively best at, even if they're not absolutely best.

Paul Samuelson called comparative advantage one of the few results in economics that's both 'true and non-trivial.' It remains the foundation of trade theory, even as modern extensions add scale economies, product differentiation, and firm heterogeneity.

concepts.title: The Labor Theory of Value
concepts.contentHtml:
The classical economists (Smith, Ricardo, and later Marx) all worked with versions of a labor theory of value: the value of a good is determined by the labor required to produce it.

Ricardo's version: in equilibrium, a good's price reflects its labor content (modified for capital, land, and time).

The labor theory captured something important — long-run prices do roughly track production costs, of which labor is a major component. It also undergirded a powerful moral framework — workers create value; if profits exist, they're taken from workers.

The marginalist revolution (1870s) replaced labor theory with marginal utility theory: value comes from how much an additional unit is worth to consumers, not from the labor that produced it. Diamonds and water — the classic puzzle — got a clean answer: water is more useful in total but the marginal liter is worth less because we have so much of it.

Modern economics largely accepts marginalism. But the labor theory's moral framework persists in Marxian and some heterodox economics, and labor-versus-capital tensions remain politically central.

title: Marxian Economics
description: Surplus value, alienation, crises of capitalism, the falling rate of profit

concepts.title: Marx in Context
concepts.contentHtml:
Karl Marx wrote in mid-19th-century Europe — early industrialization, dramatic urban growth, harsh factory labor, recurring economic crises. Das Kapital Volume 1 (1867) was the first systematic analytic critique of capitalism written from within the economic tradition.

Marx took Ricardo's labor theory of value seriously and asked: if labor creates value, where do profits come from? His answer became the analytical core of Marxian economics.

Marx wasn't writing as a moralist outside economics — he was working in the same tradition as Smith and Ricardo, with similar tools, drawing different conclusions.

Whether his analytical claims hold up is contested. But the framework of class, exploitation, and structural crisis has shaped political economy ever since.

concepts.title: Surplus Value
concepts.contentHtml:
Marx's core analytical claim: under capitalism, workers produce more value than they receive in wages. The difference is surplus value, captured by capitalists as profit.

The mechanism: a worker is paid the value needed for their reproduction (subsistence wage). But during a working day, the worker produces output worth more than that wage. The excess is surplus value.

For Marx, this was structural exploitation — not in the colloquial sense of being treated badly, but in the technical sense that workers create more value than they receive.

The labor theory of value is the load-bearing assumption. If value comes from labor, then any return to capital is value taken from labor. If value comes from utility (the marginalist view), capital's return is just compensation for capital's contribution to production.

The disagreement is foundational. Modern economics has largely sided with marginalism, but Marx's framework still shapes labor-relations debates.

concepts.title: Alienation
concepts.contentHtml:
Beyond economic exploitation, Marx argued capitalism produces alienation: workers become estranged from their work, their products, each other, and themselves.

Four dimensions:

From product: what you make is sold to someone else; you don't own or use it.

From process: you don't control how work is done; managers do.

From self: you become an instrument of someone else's purposes.

– From others: social relations are mediated through markets and money rather than direct connection.

The alienation thesis influenced not just economics but sociology, political theory, and 20th-century critical theory. Even people who reject Marx's economic analysis often find his account of work life under industrial capitalism compelling.

Modern echoes: discussions of meaningful work, gig economy precarity, technological dehumanization, and worker voice in firms.

concepts.title: Crises and the Falling Rate of Profit
concepts.contentHtml:
Marx saw capitalism as inherently unstable. Recurring crises — overproduction, financial collapse, mass unemployment — were structural, not anomalous.

His mechanism: the falling rate of profit. As capitalism develops, firms substitute capital (machines) for labor. But (in Marx's framework) only labor produces surplus value. So as the capital-to-labor ratio rises, the profit rate must fall.

Empirically, profit rates have fluctuated over capitalist history without trending sharply downward. But the broader crisis-prone-ness of capitalism — booms followed by busts, financial crises every 10-20 years — has been an enduring feature.

Modern crisis theory (Minsky, Keynes, Reinhart-Rogoff) uses different mechanisms but reaches similar empirical conclusions about capitalism's instability. Whether you call this Marx being right about the diagnosis or wrong about the mechanism is a matter of interpretation.

concepts.title: Marx's Lasting Influence
concepts.contentHtml:
Most academic economists reject Marx's specific analytical claims (the labor theory, the falling rate of profit). His broader influence on social science is enormous.

Concepts that originated with or were sharpened by Marx:

– Class as an analytical category.

– Capital accumulation as the engine of capitalism.

– Modes of production as historical organizing categories.

– Crisis-tendency of capitalism.

– Critique of commodity fetishism.

– Power relations within firms and markets.

Even mainstream economics that rejects Marx's frame uses concepts (capital, labor, exploitation, crisis) Marx helped articulate.

Politically, Marxian thought launched movements ranging from constitutional social democracies (which absorbed Marxian critiques into reformist programs) to communist revolutions (which produced the Soviet Union, Maoist China, and other totalitarian outcomes).

Whatever you think of Marx's analytical economics, the political and intellectual history of the 20th century is incomprehensible without him.

title: Marginalist Revolution
description: Jevons, Menger, Walras — utility, marginal analysis, general equilibrium

concepts.title: The Three Independent Discoveries
concepts.contentHtml:
In the 1870s, three economists working independently discovered the same insight: economic decisions are made on the margin.

– William Stanley Jevons, England, Theory of Political Economy (1871).

– Carl Menger, Austria, Principles of Economics (1871).

– Léon Walras, Switzerland, Elements of Pure Economics (1874).

All three argued that value comes from marginal utility — the satisfaction from one additional unit — not from labor content or any objective property of the good.

The simultaneous discovery suggests the idea was 'in the air' — a response to limits in classical economics that practitioners were beginning to see. The shift was so fundamental that it's called the marginalist revolution.

concepts.title: The Diamond-Water Paradox Solved
concepts.contentHtml:
Classical economists were puzzled: water is essential for life, yet cheap. Diamonds are useless ornaments, yet expensive. How can value diverge so much from usefulness?

The marginalist answer is elegant. Water is abundant; the marginal liter is worth almost nothing because we already have so much. Diamonds are scarce; the marginal diamond is worth a lot because each addition is meaningful.

Total utility (water > diamonds) and marginal utility (water < diamonds) can move in opposite directions when quantities differ. Prices reflect marginal utility, not total utility.

This single insight resolved the paradox that had vexed classical economists. It also opened the door to systematic mathematical analysis, since marginal quantities are exactly what calculus handles best.
mathExpressions: P = MU \text{ at the consumer's margin}

concepts.title: Why Marginal Thinking Matters
concepts.contentHtml:
Marginal analysis is now so deeply embedded in economic reasoning that it's easy to forget how revolutionary it was.

Pre-marginalist economics asked questions like: 'What is the value of labor?' or 'What determines wages in general?' These yielded confused or contradictory answers.

Marginalist economics asks: 'What's the value of one additional hour of labor?' or 'How does wage change with one more worker?' The marginal questions have clean answers.

The principle generalizes everywhere. Want to know whether to produce one more unit? Compare marginal cost to marginal revenue. Want to know whether to study one more hour? Compare marginal benefit to marginal cost. Want to know whether to add a worker? Compare marginal product to wage.

'Optimization on the margin' is the unifying methodological principle of modern economics. It applies wherever choices are made.

concepts.title: Walras and General Equilibrium
concepts.contentHtml:
Léon Walras took marginalism furthest. His Elements proposed: think of the entire economy as a system of simultaneous equations.

Each market has supply and demand functions. Supplies and demands depend on all prices. In general equilibrium, all markets clear simultaneously — supply equals demand everywhere.

Walras's question: does such an equilibrium exist? Does the market system have a coherent answer to the coordination problem?

His answer: yes, given enough conditions. He sketched mathematical proofs (later sharpened by Arrow and Debreu in the 1950s — Nobel Prizes).

The Arrow-Debreu general equilibrium model is one of the great theoretical achievements of 20th-century economics. It shows formally that decentralized markets can coordinate complex production and consumption — provided strong assumptions hold.

Critics argue the assumptions never hold in practice — the model is too idealized to describe real economies. Defenders argue it's the right benchmark for understanding when and why markets fail. The debate continues.

concepts.title: From Political Economy to Economics
concepts.contentHtml:
The marginalist revolution accompanied a broader change: from political economy to economics.

Classical economists wrote sweepingly about wealth, growth, distribution, history, politics, and morality. Marshall, Walras, and the marginalists narrowed the scope to formal analysis of choice under constraints.

Alfred Marshall's Principles of Economics (1890) crystallized the modern field — partial-equilibrium analysis, consumer-producer surplus, demand curves, the supply-demand cross. Marshall used 'economics' rather than 'political economy' deliberately. The discipline became more like physics, less like philosophy.

Gains: rigor, mathematics, accumulation of testable results.

Losses: scope, attention to power, engagement with normative questions, willingness to engage broader social phenomena.

The 20th century saw cycles of expansion and contraction: Keynes broadened scope; Becker extended economics into family, crime, and discrimination; behavioral economics has reintroduced psychology. The discipline keeps wrestling with how broad to be.

title: Keynesian Revolution
description: The General Theory — effective demand, animal spirits, the state as macroeconomic actor

concepts.title: The Great Depression
concepts.contentHtml:
The 1930s broke classical economics. US unemployment hit 25%. Output fell ~30%. Prices fell. The economy stayed depressed for years despite low interest rates. None of this fit the classical view that markets self-correct.

Classical theory said: in a downturn, wages and prices fall, real interest rates fall, investment recovers, employment returns. The 1930s did half of that — wages and prices did fall — but the recovery didn't follow.

John Maynard Keynes's The General Theory of Employment, Interest, and Money (1936) was the response. It argued that the classical mechanism could fail. Aggregate demand could remain depressed indefinitely without policy intervention.

The book is famously hard to read — Keynes was working out a new framework as he wrote. But its core ideas reshaped macroeconomics and economic policy for half a century.

concepts.title: Effective Demand
concepts.contentHtml:
Keynes's central concept: effective demand. Output is determined by the demand firms expect — not by potential supply.

If firms expect weak demand, they produce less, hire fewer workers, and consumers (now unemployed) buy less. The economy can settle into a self-reinforcing low-output equilibrium.

Classical economics assumed Say's Law: 'supply creates its own demand' — production generates the income that buys it. Keynes denied this. Some income goes to savings, which doesn't automatically translate into investment. The gap creates demand shortfall.

The implication: demand-side policy matters. Government can boost demand directly (spending) or indirectly (monetary stimulus, tax cuts). When private demand collapses, public demand can fill the gap.

This was the analytical foundation for both Keynes's rejection of austerity in depressions and the macro-policy framework of the postwar period.

concepts.title: Animal Spirits
concepts.contentHtml:
Keynes popularized the old phrase animal spirits for the non-rational drivers of investment.

Investment requires forecasting future returns over years or decades. The future is genuinely uncertain — not just risky in some calculable sense, but fundamentally unknowable. Investors can't compute expected returns; they form beliefs based on intuition, mood, and herd behavior.

When animal spirits are high, investment booms. When they collapse — as in 1929 — investment dries up regardless of interest rates or 'fundamentals.'

This challenged the assumption that markets aggregate rational expectations. If beliefs are partly animal spirits — emotional, social, sometimes baseless — markets can swing far from any 'fundamental' value.

Modern echoes: behavioral finance, narrative economics (Shiller), bubble-and-crash dynamics, the post-2008 understanding that investor beliefs have causal power independent of underlying conditions.

concepts.title: Liquidity Trap
concepts.contentHtml:
Keynes identified a specific failure mode of monetary policy: the liquidity trap.

At very low interest rates, additional monetary expansion fails to stimulate. Why? People simply hoard the new money rather than spending or investing it. The transmission from money to demand breaks down.

Conventional monetary policy (cutting rates, expanding money supply) becomes impotent. Only fiscal policy — direct government spending — can boost demand.

Japan after 1990 was the textbook case. Despite zero interest rates and aggressive monetary expansion, the economy stagnated. The US, UK, and eurozone hit liquidity-trap conditions after 2008. The post-pandemic period 2020-21 was different — rates near zero but high private demand.

The liquidity trap is the deepest case for fiscal stimulus over monetary stimulus. It also motivated unconventional monetary tools (QE, forward guidance) attempting to bypass conventional channels when they fail.

concepts.title: Keynesian Triumph and Decline
concepts.contentHtml:
Keynesian economics dominated postwar macroeconomic thinking and policy. The 1950s-60s saw stable growth, low unemployment, mild business cycles — what was called the 'New Economics' triumph.

The 1970s broke it. Stagflation — high inflation and high unemployment together — wasn't supposed to happen in Keynesian models. The Phillips curve relationship that Keynesians had relied on shifted unfavorably.

Friedman, Lucas, and others provided alternatives. Monetarism explained inflation as monetary phenomenon. Rational expectations argued policy effects were undermined by rational anticipation. Real business cycle theory argued that fluctuations weren't demand-driven.

By the 1980s, Keynesianism was in retreat in academic economics. New Keynesian work in the 1990s rebuilt the framework with microfoundations and rational expectations, but the political dominance of Keynesian thought weakened.

The 2008 crisis brought Keynes back. Aggregate demand matters; fiscal stimulus works in deep recessions; the zero lower bound is real — these became consensus again. The post-2008 stimulus, the post-pandemic stimulus, and modern macroeconomic policy all reflect a Keynesian inheritance, even when the term is rarely used. The framework keeps proving useful in crises.

title: Monetarist, Austrian, Chicago
description: Friedman, Hayek, rational expectations — the postwar counter-revolutions

concepts.title: Friedman and Monetarism
concepts.contentHtml:
Milton Friedman (Nobel 1976) led the monetarist counter-revolution against Keynesian dominance.

Core claim: inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon. Sustained inflation requires sustained money-supply growth above output growth. Period. Cost-push, wage-push, supply shock explanations are at best transitory contributions.

Friedman and Schwartz's A Monetary History of the United States (1963) was the key empirical work. Their reinterpretation of the Great Depression — as caused mostly by Fed monetary contraction, not by Keynes's animal spirits collapse — reframed how the era was understood.

The policy implication: don't try to fine-tune the economy with discretionary policy. Set a stable money-supply growth rule and let markets handle the rest. Friedman's k-percent rule.

Influence: huge. The 1970s-80s saw central banks broadly adopt monetarist frameworks (Volcker's disinflation, ECB's monetary pillar). The pure rule has weakened, but the underlying view that monetary policy primarily affects nominal variables — not real ones — over the long run remains mainstream.

concepts.title: The Permanent Income Hypothesis
concepts.contentHtml:
Friedman's other major contribution: the permanent income hypothesis (PIH).

Consumption decisions, Friedman argued, depend on long-run expected income, not current income. People smooth consumption over their lifetime, saving in flush years and dissaving in lean ones.

Implications:

– Tax rebates have small spending effects, because households perceive them as temporary. (Evidence is contested: Parker et al. (2013) found sizeable spending from the 2008 stimulus payments.)

– Permanent tax cuts have larger effects than temporary ones.

– Consumption is more stable than income — empirically true.

– The Keynesian consumption-income relationship was misspecified.

The PIH is one of the most successful theoretical predictions in 20th-century economics. It also undermined parts of the Keynesian fiscal-multiplier framework, which assumed temporary fiscal stimulus would translate fully into consumption.

Modern variants — buffer-stock saving, life-cycle models with credit constraints — refine the basic PIH while keeping its core insight.

concepts.title: Hayek and the Austrian School
concepts.contentHtml:
Friedrich Hayek (Nobel 1974) developed a different critique of mainstream economics.

His central concern: the knowledge problem. The information needed to coordinate an economy — millions of individual preferences, technologies, locations — is dispersed and tacit. No central authority can ever assemble it. Markets work because they aggregate this dispersed knowledge through prices.

This argument cut against centrally planned economies (Soviet-style) but also against extensive Keynesian fine-tuning. Even well-intentioned planners lack the information to do better than the price system.

The Road to Serfdom (1944) connected economic to political freedom: when government takes over economic coordination, it inevitably takes over political life too.

Austrian economics (Mises, Hayek, Rothbard, others) emphasizes:

– Subjective theories of value.

– The market as a process of discovery, not equilibrium.

– Skepticism of mathematical formalism in economics.

– Strong libertarian policy implications.

The Austrian school has influence outside academic mainstream economics, particularly in libertarian political thought.

concepts.title: Rational Expectations
concepts.contentHtml:
Robert Lucas (Nobel 1995) led the rational expectations revolution in the 1970s.

The core idea: in models, agents shouldn't form expectations naively. They should use the model itself to forecast. If the central bank announces a stimulus, rational agents anticipate the inflation and adjust prices and wages accordingly — undermining the stimulus's real effects.

Implication: predictable policy effects are mostly absorbed by expectation adjustments. Only surprises have real effects, and surprises tend to wash out over time.

The Lucas critique: don't naively extrapolate behavioral parameters from historical data, because those parameters depend on the policy regime. Change the regime, and you change the parameters.

Combined with Friedman's permanent-income work, rational expectations transformed macroeconomics. Old Keynesian models were rebuilt with microfoundations and forward-looking expectations. New Classical economics took rational expectations to libertarian conclusions; New Keynesian economics absorbed it while keeping demand-management implications.

By the 1990s, mainstream macro was largely 'New Neoclassical Synthesis' — RBC framework with sticky prices, rational expectations, and DSGE modeling. The 2008 crisis shook this framework's confidence; rebuilding is ongoing.

concepts.title: Modern Synthesis and Open Questions
concepts.contentHtml:
Where does economic thought stand today?

The mainstream synthesis includes:

– Marginalist methodology (optimization, equilibrium).

– Rational expectations as a benchmark, with bounded-rationality refinements.

– Monetary policy as primary stabilization tool, fiscal as secondary.

– Markets work but have important failures (externalities, public goods, asymmetric information).

– Long-run growth driven by technology and institutions.

Active debates and unsettled questions:

– Inequality and wealth concentration: what mechanisms, what consequences, what policies? Piketty's revival of the question.

– Climate and the long run: how to integrate environmental constraints into growth models.

– The role of finance: is the financial sector productive or rent-extracting?

– Behavioral revolution: how much should standard models incorporate psychological realism?

– Inflation dynamics: the post-2021 episode has reopened questions about what causes inflation and how to control it.

Economics, like any live science, is unfinished. The history of thought is the long story of asking better questions, even when answers stay elusive.
